title: Littlebell: How to Spot and Control This Vine in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Littlebell in Rice: Spot and Control This Climbing Weed
metaDescription: Littlebell, or aurora, is a twining vine with heart shaped leaves and pink flowers in rainfed rice. Learn to spot it and pull it before it seeds.
excerpt: Littlebell is a small twining vine with heart shaped leaves and pink to purple flowers. Many farmers know it as aurora or kamkamote. It grows in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it and how it wraps around and competes with your palay. Then it shows how to control it before it sets seed.

heroImage.alt: Littlebell (Ipomoea triloba), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields

blocks.text:
Littlebell is an annual vine from the morning glory family, Convolvulaceae, so it is a relative of kamote and kangkong. Its thin stems either twine around other plants or crawl along the ground. Farmers have many names for it, such as aurora, bangbangau, kamkamote, koskusipa, kupit kupit, halobagbug and muti muti. Its scientific name is Ipomoea triloba.

You will find this damo in rainfed lowland rice fields. Since it is an annual, its life lasts one season only. Within one crop it sprouts, climbs, flowers, sets seed and dies. Seed is its only way to spread. Once a flower fades, it can turn into a small round pod with a few seeds inside. Those seeds stay in the soil until the next crop, and then they come up again.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about littlebell
rows: Aurora, bangbangau, kamkamote, koskusipa, kupit kupit, halobagbug, muti muti

blocks.text: Look for thin stems that twist around rice stalks or crawl over the soil. The leaves are broad and oval, with a heart shaped base and a long pointed tip. Some leaves are whole, while others show three shallow lobes. Like other broadleaf weeds, the leaves are wide with netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. Its small bell shaped flowers are pink to purple.

items: Thin vine stems twisting around rice stalks or crawling across the ground.
Broad, oval leaves with a heart shaped base and a long pointed tip.
Leaves that are whole or show three shallow lobes, a bit like a small kamote leaf.
Small pink to purple flowers shaped like little bells or funnels.
Rice hills pulled together or bent where the vine has wrapped around them.

blocks.text:
This vine competes with your palay in two ways. First, like any weed, it takes sunlight, water and fertilizer from the soil your rice shares. Next, its twining stems wrap around rice plants. The vine climbs up the stalks, spreads its leaves over the crop and adds shade where the rice needs light.

A tangled vine also makes work harder. It slows hand weeding and can get caught at harvest. Since it is an annual that spreads by seed, each vine that flowers adds seed to your soil for next season. Seeds can also end up mixed in the harvested palay.

items: Unwind the vine from the rice gently and pull it out by the root. Pulling works better than cutting off the top.
Weed early, before the stems twine up the rice. Young vines lying on the ground are much easier to remove.
Remove vines before the pink flowers turn into pods, so no new seeds fall into the paddy.
Clear the bunds and fence lines too, since vines there can climb, flower and drop seed into the field.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold littlebell down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

items.q: What do farmers call littlebell in the Philippines?
items.a: It has many local names. Depending on the place, farmers call it aurora, bangbangau, kamkamote, koskusipa, kupit kupit, halobagbug or muti muti. The name kamkamote fits, because it is a relative of kamote. In English it is littlebell, and its scientific name is Ipomoea triloba.

items.q: How do I control aurora vine in my rice field?
items.a: Start with prevention. Prepare the land well, use clean binhi, and keep water in the paddy when rain allows. Weed early, before the vines twine up the rice, and pull each one out by the root. If many come up, choose a herbicide for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Is kamkamote the same as kamote?
items.a: No. It belongs to the same family as kamote, and its leaves can look alike, so some farmers call it kamkamote. But it is a different plant. It is an annual vine with thin stems and small pink to purple flowers, and it does not form the big roots we harvest. In your rice field, treat it as a weed.
